Photograph: BBC UK news Five men arrested at RAF Fairford are all UK nationals from London, say police Officers say they have secured extension to continue to hold men, all in their 20s, on suspicion of terror offences Helena Horton Mon 28 Sep 2026 07.56 EDT Last modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 08.10 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Five men arrested on suspicion of terror offences at RAF Fairford are all British nationals from London in their 20s, counter-terrorism police have said. The men were pictured on Sunday being apprehended, shirtless, near the RAF base in Gloucestershire, which is being used by the US air force in its operations against Iran. Three of them were 24, one was 25 and one 23, and three resided in Westminster, another in Camden, and another in Willseden, police said. Officers said they were being held under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act and a custody extension had been secured until later on Monday. The suspects were arrested in Whelford on Sunday morning after reports of three vehicles travelling towards the airbase at 12.45am. They were detained on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act and preparation of a terrorist act contrary to section 5 of the Terrorism Act. Counter-terrorism policing said investigators were examining the scene overnight and had been carrying out a range of activity that had led to multiple new lines of inquiry. View image in fullscreen Armoured vehicle on patrol at RAF Fairford on Monday. Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty Images Eighty-five households were evacuated from the village on Sunday, and a large police and emergency services presence has been there ever since. Police said they were using “significant numbers of resources, including military assets” at the location, adding: “We are working hard to minimise disruption to local communities, but ask for their patience, as our work continues at the scene.” Deputy assistant commissioner Vicki Evans, the Counter Terrorism Policing enior national coordinator, said: “This is a hugely complex and large-scale operation, involving local and national policing, the MoD [Ministry of Defence], and local agencies, who are working together to progress the investigation and support for the community. “I know this has been incredibly disruptive for local people, but I’d like to reassure them that our activity is in the interest of national security, but most importantly in the interest of their own safety. “I am very aware of the levels of speculation about the motivation behind this incident, and the geopolitical questions that are being raised. However, I ask that at this time, Counter Terrorism Policing are given the space to work carefully and clearly.” There is still a cordon in place at the location but police said they would be reviewing it later today. Log in here » NOVI SAD, Serbia (AP) — A week after a student movement toppled Serbia’s strongman Aleksandar Vucic in an election, thousands of students and their supporters on Sunday marked two years since a deadly train station disaster that gave birth to their anti-corruption campaign. The demand for accountability over the Nov. 1, 2024 collapse of a concrete canopy at the station in the northern city of Novi Sad that killed 16 people launched two years of student-led protests that eventually brought about the stunning defeat of Vucic’s right-wing government at last week’s parliamentary elections. In steady rain and silence, thousands marched in Novi Sad on Sunday in a gesture of respect for the victims. Unlike a year ago, when huge crowds gathered for the first anniversary of the tragedy, participants this year said they now have hope that those responsible for the disaster will be punished. A rose is placed outside the train station in Novi Sad, Serbia, Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, on the second anniversary of the canopy collapse disaster that killed 16 people. (AP Photo/Darko Vojinovic) The students brought 16 wreaths and 16 red hearts — one for each victim — outside the station building. The inscribed names of the victims included children. People cried as they laid down flowers and lit candles. A moment of silence was held. A struggle against corruption was at the center of the student uprising Many in Serbia believe that the concrete canopy crashed because of flawed renovation work caused by corruption and negligence that prevailed in major state infrastructure projects championed by Vucic’s government. The station renovation was part of a bigger railway reconstruction project with China and neighboring Hungary. Vucic and his ally, former right-wing Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban together toured the renewed Novi Sad station back in 2022. “It was a murder and a murder demands accountability and justice,” a student said in a speech Sunday, promising that Serbia’s young people will build a more just society in the future. “We will not forget them (victims).” Since the election in which the Students’ List defeated Vucic’s long-ruling Serbian Progressive Party, or SNS, last Sunday, the students have demanded a review of high-profile investigations, including the probe into the canopy collapse. Previously, 13 people had been charged, including a government minister, but no trial was held as the probe stalled. The head of the European Union mission in Serbia, Andreas von Beckerath, wrote on X that the canopy collapse “shook Serbia to its core and moved citizens across the country to demand transparency and accountability.” “May their memory keep inspiring a Serbia built on solidarity, public trust and rule of law,” he added. Also Sunday, prosecutors ordered a 48-hour detention of Marko Kricak, Vucic’s chief of criminal police. Another senior officer was detained along with Kricak, both on suspicion of abuse of office in connection with a murder investigation. Kricak was accused of orchestrating violence during the student protests, and of personally threatening a female student with rape, allegations that he has denied. After it took office 14 years ago, Vucic’s SNS party gradually took control of all state institutions. The students’ movement has promised to restore the rule of law and democracy, and root out rampant graft that they say flourished under Vucic. The station tragedy became a symbol of the struggle for rule of law On Nov. 1, 2024, the huge concrete construction at the outer front wall of the Novi Sad station crashed without warning at 11:52 a.m., crushing people underneath as they were waiting for trains on a sunny autumn day. Fourteen people died at the scene, and two died later. A young woman survived with life-changing injuries. Authorities first said that the canopy had not been renovated at all, and promised an investigation. But protests started almost immediately with people blocking traffic every day across the country at the exact time of the collapse and demanding justice. Some of the student-led rallies held in the last two years were among the biggest anti-government protests in Serbia’s history. And unlike last year when Vucic was in power, Sunday’s anniversary memorial was broadcast by state RTS television, following resignations among officials at the TV station in the post-election week. Commemoration ceremonies were also held in other cities and towns throughout Serbia. An independent investigation by a group of experts into the canopy collapse found the renovation work had been rushed under political orders. The experts’ report alleged a “systematic degradation of construction standards” and said that the “state of Serbia violated its citizens’ right to life.” Advertisement Advertise With Us Advertisement Advertise With Us Tweet Share Print Email Read Later Report Error Submit a Tip Advertisement Learn more about Winnipeg Free Press Advertising solutions World LOAD WORLD ARTICLES

A megszerzett dokumentumok alapján az újságírók szeptemberig bezárólag legalább 490 ezer, az orosz állam által is hivatalosan regisztrált katonai halálesetet azonosítottak. Az állami adminisztrációban azonban jelentős késéssel jelennek meg az adatok, így a nyilvántartás a 2026-os halálesetek többségét és a 2025-ös veszteségek egy jó részét még nem tartalmazza. Ezt az adminisztratív csúszást tudományos előrejelzési módszerekkel korrigálták a kutatók. Kiszámították, mekkora lenne a tényleges veszteség, ha a rendszer teljesen naprakész lenne, és beleszámították azokat a hivatalosan eltűntként nyilvántartott katonákat is, akik nagy valószínűséggel már nem élnek. Így jutottak el a 700 ezret is meghaladó számhoz, amely csak az elesetteket jelöli, a sebesültekre nem tér ki. A The New York Times ugyanakkor jelezte, hogy független forrásból nem tudta megerősíteni az elemzés hitelességét. Az információk közvetlenül az orosz állami statisztikai szolgálattól, a Roszsztattól származnak. A két szerkesztőség évek óta követi nyomon az orosz veszteségeket, elsősorban hagyatéki eljárások és gyászjelentések alapján, ám a mostani adatszivárgás révén hozzáfértek az anyakönyvi hivatalok és a kormányzati adatcsererendszer anonimizált nyilvántartásaihoz is. Michael Kofman, a Carnegie Nemzetközi Békekutató Alapítvány vezető kutatója szerint Oroszország jelenleg több katonát veszít, mint amennyit pótolni tud, ám a kiemelkedő pénzügyi juttatásoknak köszönhetően Moszkva így is képes lesz mintegy 409 ezer új embert toborozni 2026-ban. Ez a tempó elegendő a veszteségek pótlására és a harcok fenntartására, arra azonban már nem, hogy az orosz hadsereg javítson a harctéri pozícióin. A szakértő szerint a Kreml előbb-utóbb kifogyhat a rohamgyalogságból, és ha nem változtatnak a csapatok bevetési taktikáján, a befektetett erőforrások egyre kisebb eredményt hoznak majd.
